title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time in Italian, make plans for a set time, and cope with the 24-hour clock on official timetables.
bekal: tell the time with *sono le* and the exception *è l'una*
tell *che ore sono* (what time is it) from *a che ora* (what time does it happen)
read train and movie timetables that use the 24-hour clock

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Un appuntamento
dialogs.intro: Giulia and Budi are arranging to see a movie. Notice the two different questions about time in the first and fourth lines.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Così tardi! Il film comincia presto?
lines.id: That late! Does the movie start early?
lines.literal: so late! the film begins early?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: A che ora vuoi andare? C'è alle sei e alle otto e un quarto.
lines.id: What time do you want to go? There's one at six and one at a quarter past eight.
lines.literal: at what hour you-want to-go? there-is at-the six and at-the eight and a quarter.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Alle otto è meglio. Finisco di lavorare alle sette.
lines.id: Eight is better. I finish work at seven.
lines.literal: at-the eight is better. I-finish of to-work at-the seven.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Perfetto. Ci vediamo alle otto meno dieci davanti al cinema.
lines.id: Perfect. See you at ten to eight in front of the movie theater.
lines.literal: perfect. us we-see at-the eight minus ten in-front to-the cinema.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Va bene. E dopo? I bar chiudono a mezzanotte?
lines.id: OK. And afterwards? Do the bars close at midnight?
lines.literal: goes well. and after? the bars they-close at midnight?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Alcuni sì. Ma il locale vicino chiude all'una.
lines.id: Some do. But the place nearby closes at one.
lines.literal: some yes. but the place near closes at-the one.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ah, il biglietto dice ventidue e trenta. Che ora è?
lines.id: Oh, the ticket says 22:30. What time is that?
lines.literal: ah, the ticket says twenty-two and thirty. what hour is?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Le dieci e mezza di sera. Gli orari ufficiali usano le ventiquattro ore.
lines.id: Half past ten at night. Official timetables use the 24-hour clock.
lines.literal: the ten and half of evening. the timetables official they-use the twenty-four hours.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Capito. Allora a stasera, alle otto meno dieci!
lines.id: Got it. See you tonight then, at ten to eight!
lines.literal: understood. then until this-evening, at-the eight minus ten!

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: A stasera! E non fare tardi!
lines.id: See you tonight! And don't be late!
lines.literal: until this-evening! and not to-make late!

notes: **Sono le, not è le.** Times are plural because what's really meant is *le ore* — the hours. So the verb is plural: *sono le tre*, *sono le otto*.
**Except for three singular times.** *È l'una* (one o'clock), *è mezzogiorno* (noon), *è mezzanotte* (midnight). All three take *è*, because there's only one of each.

**Che ore sono vs a che ora.** The first asks the time now. The second asks when something happens: *A che ora comincia il film?* Mixing them up is a mistake people hear at once. *Che ora è?* is also correct and means the same as *che ore sono?*.
**Answer "at what time" with alle.** *Alle otto*, *all'una*, *a mezzogiorno*. Notice how *a* merges with the article — exactly the merging that's unpacked in Unit 10.
**Minutes are added with e and subtracted with meno.** *Le otto e dieci* (ten past eight), *le otto meno dieci* (ten to eight). After the half hour, Italians usually count down to the next hour.

**Le tre e mezza = half past three.** Here Italian works just like English: the hour first, then the minutes added on. (If you know some German, forget *halb vier* — Italian never counts the half toward the next hour.)

**The 24-hour clock is used on all official timetables.** Trains, planes, movie theaters, offices: *le quattordici e trenta* for 14:30. In everyday conversation people still use the 12-hour clock and add *di mattina*, *di pomeriggio*, *di sera*, *di notte*.
**Non fare tardi** = don't be late. This is the negative command, which in the informal form uses *non* + the infinitive. Commands are unpacked in Unit 16.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: One pattern for almost everything, plus three exceptions to learn.

head: Time
Italiano
Note
rows: Sono le tre e un quarto.
Sono le quattro meno un quarto.
Sono le sette e venti di sera.

after: The forms *e quindici*, *e trenta*, *e quarantacinque* are always safe and never wrong. If you're not yet sure of *meno* and *mezza*, just use the numbers for now.

grammars.title: Parts of the day
body: To make clear whether a 12-hour time is morning or night, Italians tack on the part of the day.
after: The boundaries aren't fixed, and Italians themselves disagree, especially about when *pomeriggio* ends. What matters is that you get your meaning across.
Notice that *sera* stretches late, to about eleven — so "nine at night" is still *le nove di sera*. A dinner invitation *alle otto di sera* is an ordinary dinner, not a late one.

blocks.text: Watch *mai*: it needs *non* in front of the verb. *Non arrivo mai tardi* is literally "I don't arrive never late". In English that double negative is "wrong"; in Italian it's correct and required.

blocks.title: Making plans
items: *A che ora ci vediamo?* — What time shall we meet?
*Ci vediamo alle otto.* — Let's meet at eight.
*Va bene alle sette?* — Is seven OK?
*Sono in ritardo, scusa.* — I'm late, sorry.
*Arrivo tra dieci minuti.* — I'll be there in ten minutes.
*Facciamo più tardi?* — Shall we make it later?

exercises.prompt: Fill in che ore sono or a che ora.
